common_name: Alexander's Surprise Moss Phlox (Parent of Nettleton's Variation)

planting.note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; Alexander's Surprise is the parent cultivar from which the variegated sport Nettleton's Variation later arose.

directions: Set out container-grown plants in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, where the plant forms a dense, needle-leaved evergreen mat typical of moss phlox. In mid to late spring it disappears under a solid flush of salmon-pink flowers with a darker pink eye at the center of each bloom, a color combination that has kept it popular with alpine and rock-garden growers for decades. Unlike its later sport Nettleton's Variation, the foliage here stays plain green year-round rather than cream-edged. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight, and avoid heavy, poorly drained soils that invite crown rot over winter.

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall in well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; Queen Fabiola is the best-known selection of triplet lily, chosen for larger umbels and deeper violet-blue color than the wild species.

directions: Plant corms in fall in gritty, well-drained soil that bakes dry through summer, since Queen Fabiola shares its parent species' absolute need for a dry dormant season. In late spring it sends up wiry stems topped with unusually large umbels of upright, bell-shaped, sky-blue flowers striped with darker navy veining, a richer and showier display than the species type. Plant corms in generous drifts rather than singly, since scattered plants read as sparse against open ground. It naturalizes well in dry slopes, gravel gardens, and Mediterranean-climate borders, and reliably attracts butterflies and hummingbirds while needing no summer irrigation at all.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

common_name: Driftwood Spuria Iris (Chocolate Brown and Gold Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter; Driftwood was bred by Marion Walker, introduced in the 1950s, later used as a parent of 'Imperial Bronze', and holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Driftwood carries rich chocolate-brown standards over falls heavily overlaid in golden yellow, a warm, earthy color break that stood out among the mostly blue and yellow spurias available when it was introduced. Tall, sturdy stems hold the midseason flowers well above narrow, upright foliage. Water generously from fall regrowth through the spring bloom period, then let the soil dry out through the plant's summer dormancy to avoid rhizome rot. Feed in early spring and leave established clumps undisturbed for several years, since spurias resent frequent division and can sulk for a season or two afterward.

common_name: Imperial Night Spuria Iris (Deep Purple Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall in full sun; Imperial Night was bred by Eleanor McCown and registered in the 1960s, and was later crossed with 'Driftwood' to produce the cultivar 'Imperial Bronze'.

directions: Imperial Night bears self-colored, deep velvety purple flowers on tall stems in midseason, a saturated, almost blackish tone that reads as one of the darkest shades available among spuria irises. Narrow, ribbed, sword-like foliage stays upright and tidy through the growing season. Keep the planting consistently moist from fall through spring bloom, then withhold water during midsummer dormancy, since standing moisture at that time invites rot. Fertilize lightly in early spring and avoid disturbing established clumps, since spurias are slow to rebloom after being divided.

common_name: Redwood Supreme Spuria Iris (Chocolate Brown and Orange Nies Medal Parent)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall in full sun; Redwood Supreme was bred by O. David Niswonger, registered in 1976, and received an American Iris Society Honorable Mention in 1981 before going on to parent two later Nies Medal winners, 'Sultan's Sash' and 'Missouri Autumn'.

directions: Redwood Supreme shows dark chocolate-brown standards paired with orange falls edged in the same dark brown, a striking bicolor combination on tall stems in midseason. Although it only earned an Honorable Mention in its own right, it proved to be an exceptional parent, passing its distinctive coloring and vigor into two later Nies Medal-winning spurias. Water generously from fall through the spring bloom season, then allow the soil to dry through summer dormancy to prevent rhizome rot. Feed in early spring and leave clumps undisturbed for several years, since spurias resent frequent digging and need time to rebuild bloom strength after division.
